name: rebound
description: An expected-value revenue recovery agent for Razorpay merchants. Decides which at-risk rupees are worth chasing, how, when, and when to stop.

scripts.check: npm run test && npm run verify-sim && npm run diagnose-report && npm run model-report && npm run decide-report && npm run orchestrate-report && npm run eval-smoke

scripts: `decide-report` and `orchestrate-report` answer two different questions and both are in `check` on purpose. `decide-report` prints what the policy EXPECTS to recover — arithmetic over its own estimates, nothing executed. `orchestrate-report` runs the loop against the simulated gateway across several cycles and prints what a receipt actually said was captured. A regression that leaves the EV maths intact but breaks execution, scheduling or the guardrail ledger is invisible to the first and loud in the second.

`select-arm` is deliberately NOT part of `check`. It runs a 20-world sweep and takes about 90 seconds, and `check` has to stay fast enough to run on every change. The plumbing and the statistics are covered by test/armSelection.test.js, which runs the same procedure on three tiny worlds in under two seconds; the full sweep is a deliberate act you perform when choosing which model the decision engine is built on, not a per-commit check.

`select-arm` is also the only command permitted to decide that choice. `model-report` scores the reserved held-out batch and is for final reporting only — reading an arm choice out of it is what went wrong on Day 5.
dependencies: Deliberately short. `razorpay` was removed once the client was hand-rolled over fetch (see src/razorpay/httpClient.js for the reasoning), and `dotenv` once src/core/env.js replaced it.

Everything that produces a number in this project — the seeder, the simulator, the eval, the whole test suite — runs on a clean clone with zero installed packages. The two remaining entries are only needed for the API server and the persisted audit trail.
